passage: "Another rejection." Nirmala dropped her phone on the flat's only sofa. "That's the eleventh." Tenzin looked up from his laptop. "Sorry, yaar." "Every senior from the batch above got placed in campus week. Every single one. Two years ago companies were queuing up. We get a hiring freeze." "It's not your fault." "Then whose? I did everything right. I topped my section. I was promised this." Tenzin paused. "Who promised?" "Everyone! The brochure, the seniors, my uncle." Her voice cracked. "And now the second-years are getting internships at the same companies that turned me down." "That's rough." "It's more than rough. It's unfair." Tenzin closed the laptop. "The timing is unfair. Want to look at what's actually hiring, together? Tomorrow, not tonight." Nirmala stared at the ceiling. "Tomorrow."

qa.q: Which rejection was this for Nirmala?
qa.a: The eleventh rejection.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's 'I was promised this' reveal about her anger?
qa.a: She feels entitled to the job her seniors got, so the gap between expectation and reality feels like something being withheld.

qa.q: What small step does Tenzin suggest, and why is the timing wise?
qa.a: Looking together at what's actually hiring, tomorrow rather than tonight, so Nirmala can act once the anger has cooled.

qa.q: How does Tenzin seem to see Nirmala's situation?
qa.a: He sees real bad luck in the timing and cares, but gently asks who promised the job, hinting the expectation was never a guarantee.

grounding: A graduate who expected a job like her seniors' feels bitter and entitled, and angrier still as juniors seem to get what she believed was hers.

passage: I'm Farida. When I finished my commerce degree, I was sure I'd walk into a bank job, like the three seniors who had mentored me. They got offers in their final year, and I'd done better than two of them. Then, the year I graduated, the banks froze hiring. I sent out forty applications. I got two interviews and no offers. I remember sitting in Nandini's kitchen, raging. "They owe us. We did what we were told." Nandini said quietly, "Who's they?" I couldn't answer. What made it worse was watching the next batch get internships as things picked up. It felt like the line had moved just as I reached it. It took me months to separate bad luck from the belief that something had been stolen from me.

qa.q: How many applications did Farida send out?
qa.a: Forty applications.

qa.q: Why did it feel worse to Farida when the next batch got internships?
qa.a: It felt like the line had moved just as Farida reached it, making the missed job seem stolen rather than unlucky.

qa.q: What question from Nandini became a turning point, and why?
qa.a: 'Who's they?', because it made Farida see there was no one who owed the job, only bad timing.

qa.q: How might Nandini have felt listening to Farida rage in the kitchen?
qa.a: Nandini probably felt concerned and wanted to help Farida see clearly, rather than feed the anger.

grounding: A graduate who expected the jobs their seniors got feels robbed and bitter when a hiring freeze intervenes, and angrier still as the next batch benefits.

passage: Career centre note, 15 January. Written by Binita. Divyansh, twenty-two, came in for the third time this month. He graduated in civil engineering last year, the batch after the one where every student had a site job before exams. His batch met a hiring freeze. He is angry, and says so: "The seniors were no better than me. I earned that job, and it's being kept from me." When he hears that juniors are now landing internships, he goes red and stops listening. I don't doubt his ability. But the anger is making him turn down smaller openings as "beneath what I was promised." Today we listed three firms hiring for project roles and practised one interview. He agreed to apply to two. We meet again on the 29th.

qa.q: How many firms hiring for project roles did they list today?
qa.a: Three firms.

qa.q: What does Divyansh's reaction to juniors getting internships show about how he feels?
qa.a: He goes red and stops listening, showing bitterness that others seem to be getting what he believes he deserved.

qa.q: What did Binita and Divyansh do today, and why is it useful?
qa.a: They listed three firms, practised an interview, and he agreed to apply to two, turning anger into concrete steps.

qa.q: How might Divyansh's anger look to employers offering smaller openings?
qa.a: Employers may see someone who thinks their role is beneath him, missing the capable engineer behind the frustration.

grounding: A career counsellor sees a graduate who expected his seniors' kind of job feel bitter and entitled, especially as juniors get opportunities, and helps him take concrete steps.

passage:
Thursday

The nursing recruitment exam has been postponed AGAIN. Third time. No new date.

Every single senior from the batch above me got a government hospital post straight after the results. Zainab's batch, every one of them. They'd tell us in the canteen, "Don't worry, it's automatic." I topped my practicals. I did everything they did, and more. And now I'm working night shifts at a small clinic for half the pay while the seniors post photos in their new uniforms.

I'm so angry I can't sleep. It feels like someone took my post and put it in a drawer.

Zainab called tonight. She said, "Rehana, it's not personal. It's the timing." I snapped at her. Then I felt terrible. It isn't her fault she got hers.

But it isn't mine either that I didn't get mine.

qa.q: How many times has the recruitment exam been postponed?
qa.a: It has been postponed three times.

qa.q: What does Rehana mean by writing that someone took the post and put it in a drawer?
qa.a: Rehana feels bitter and as if something earned and was owed is being withheld.

qa.q: What could Rehana try after snapping at Zainab?
qa.a: Rehana could call Zainab back to apologise, and then look at what can be prepared while waiting, instead of letting anger at the seniors fill the nights.

qa.q: How might Zainab have felt when Rehana snapped at her?
qa.a: Zainab might have felt hurt, since she was trying to comfort Rehana, and a little awkward about having got a post herself.

grounding: A young graduate who expected a post like the batch above feels bitter and entitled when it does not come, especially seeing the seniors' success.
